title: thoughts on Jean-Luc Godard saying he hates zooms in film?

commenti.body: [removed]
[removed]

Zooming produces an effect. Never zooming in or out produces an effect.

Moving the camera produces an effect. Keeping the camera static produces an effect. 

Neither side is right or wrong, they just prefer different kinds of shots.
[removed]

Zooms can be overdone. John Waters said he was guilty of zoom abuse in films like Pink Flamingos. It adds to the aesthetic. Plus it was used masterfully in Vertigo or the films of Ophuls. Maybe he thought that zooms were used too much as a crutch and a cheap trick, like a jump scare in horror movies, to have style over substance. In history of cinema Godard saw Jaws as a sort of deathknell for both non formulaic American movies and non Americanized foreign films. 

Bresson and Ozu are two notable directors who didn't rely on zooms. Godard called Balthazar the world in an hour and a half. Maybe he thought zooms were mostly superfluous and condescends to the audience; maybe he thought filmmakers were resting on their laurels. Those two filmmakers represent the high watermark of spiritually significant films.

I like zooms a lot, they're fun and memorable, really practical for establishing a location and character actions in the same shot, zooming into a character's face has a wonderful dramatic flair. But I'll admit that they're for the most part one of the showier filming techniques, I can see how a filmmaker who prefers a more grounded approach would dislike them, but the idea of not using them for any film sounds incredibly dull to me. I find his reasonings in the video  pretty lacking though, the fact that TV uses zooms should have no bearing on cinema, and neither does the Lumiere brothers not inventing it, that's a terrible way to judge artistic techniques. Painters don't have a zoom but you can appreciate different details at different distances, plus it's a different artform.

Godard likes to throw out provocative statements. He has trollish tendencies, but more often than not I believe he has a genuine motivation to shake things up, challenge people to think bigger and question the status quo. Zooms became really popular in the 70s and people were using them for everything. Godard is saying, just because something is easy doesn't make it appropriate. He's saying, have artistic principles, don't do stuff just because it's trendy or expedient.

He's mistaking his own stylistic opinion for being a definitive aspect of tradecraft. He's hardly the first person to do it. I don't see this as being much different from modern big name directors whining that superhero movies aren't art.

Holy cow, these are horrible arguments. He comes off entirely arrogant, pretentious, and something of a troglodyte, the latter is particularly hypocritical given that he's working with a highly technical medium. However, as someone who is *not* a Godard fan, I believe these descriptions fit him properly.  

"It wasn't used before so why use it now" Guess what, pal, film wasn't a thing 80 years ago, so why use it now? 

"Television uses it, how good can it be?" There is nothing inherently wrong or bad about television. There may be a lot of bad television shows, but television as a medium is as valid as any other. He sees it as low art, well, guess what, pal, when film first came out it was considered low art, nearly pornographic. Things change. 

"Painters don't have zooms." Guess what, pal, they also don't have photographic film, what kind of argument is that? 

If he thinks the camera should be where it should be and never move, that's fine. Go for it. I love static shots. But, it seems like his argument should apply to moving the camera or changing composition entirely. 

Does he ever move the camera in his movies? Yes he does. I just checked '2 or 3 Things I know About Her' from 1967 (it's on Criterion.) I hopped around and found a moving camera shot at about 17 minutes. So much for not moving the camera or changing the composition. As far as I can tell, he's talking out of his ass. 

Most confusingly, it would seem one of the great advantages of cinema, something that sets it apart from painting and still photography is the ABILITY TO MOVE THE CAMERA and change composition. 

In the end, these are not intelligent arguments. They are pretentious, arrogant, and unsubstantiated. I'm now more convinced I don't need to see more of this guy's movies.

Godard has a lot of incendiary takes on cinema which don't stand up to scrutiny.  I appreciate what he's done for the art, but I'm not going to listen to film rules by the guy who got famous for breaking most of them.

He was such an insane moron. And of course there's somebody in this thread defending him by saying "zoom is too easy" and Godard wanted to challenge such things, lol. The worst part is his comments about TV. In a single episode of any TV show from the 60's or 70's, there's more genuine effort to create something meaningful than you'll ever see in any Godard film that's ever been made.

Yeah, I wouldn't put too much store by it either. He was one of the writers at *Cahiers du Cinema* who first noticed Hitchcock's great style, which of course was before he started making films. I think he was just fond of making quips and provocative, dogmatic statements. *L'Histoire(s) du Cinema* is 50% quips in big letters over (supremely well chosen) clips from old films.

Zoom lenses were around since the silent era, but they really gained traction in the mid to late 60s, so in that era that technique was everywhere from movies to TV.

So it's probably the combination of "zoom forward" burnout and the fact that prime lenses are generally sharper..

First of all, the television part was a joke. He was being filmed for a television interview and saw the camera operator using the zoom lens. 

He then goes on to say there’s some truth behind the joke, that he hates zooms, but in context it feels pretty grounded in his personal hatred of them. The Lumiere & painting point are his points of inspiration, not objectively binding.

This [essay](https://www.premiumbeat.com/blog/zoom-in-filmmaking/#:~:text=Much%20like%20an%20intrusive%20narrator,further%20into%20the%20film%20world.) is much clearer and presents the general argument against zooms, which _many_ filmmakers and cinematographers would generally agree with. It’s a general argument which allows for exceptions.

The dolly-zoom (“vertigo effect”) has a very different effect, so I don’t think it’s covered by JLG’s ire. Plus, he adored Hitchcock.

GOAT Kubrick disagrees.

I mean I get it, I used to hate them too. I think they're a more stylistic choice which makes their popularity ebb and flow with trends.

They were big from the late 60s to early 80s and have had small revivals since, one we're in the middle/tail end of.

I think as long as it's justified it can be used any time.

Like any camera movement, it's all about the intention, the context (what happens before or after the movement) and how skillfully it fits into the entire scene (editing). Personally, I find the quick zooms they liked in the late 60's/70's charming but it can also be a cheap way to "jazz up" a scene that isn't very well shot/choreographed/directed.

Over use of the zoom feature on a camera is one of the easiest ways to spot an amateur. Or at least it used to be back in the days before cellphones. If you're given a real camera to work with its one of the features you're likely to toy with the most until you get bored with it. If you watch a lot of student films you'll get annoyed with seeing it abused. It can be used masterfully. It can be avoided masterfully. Goddard is a one of the few directors with a style so unique you could tell he directed a film even if his name isn't in the credits. What he chose to use or not use is important to his vision but every filmmaker has to find what works for themselves.

It’s not a far leap to see why a systems thinker such as Godard might be inclined to show a wider scene than a tight focus on individual emotions.

Jean-Pierre Melville is not averse to employing zooms in his filmmaking. Although, his directorial style leans more towards the sensory, in contrast to the more intellectual approaches of Godard and Bresson.

It's just a outrageous strong opinion like Godard told so much as truths, and in itself, the fact that Godard says it here doesn't mean a lot.

That said, I can understand the problem with zooms, as I have them younger. Zooms have something in common with drones or CGI todays: they are a lazy substitute to "the real thing" (for each one: travelling, dolly/copter, or practical effects). And if feels. Really, it feels in front of a film, when it's used in a way which could have been possible trough a more difficult, heavy and concrete solution. You feel the weight of a travelling, the choice in it, the precision of going from there to there - and if the zoom is just there because it's cheaper, just because moving the lens is more easy than moving the all camera, the laziness of this choice feels. 

That said, zooms are also used for themselves, and not only as travelling substitutes. Utlra-speed zooms pointing something in Shaw brothers movie, for instance, are something else. Slow zoom in *Barry Lyndon*, crushing the perspectives, making the images lika a flat painting, or mathematically/coldly pointing something, have their own dreamy characteristics a travelling wouldn't have. Etc.
[removed]

Godard uses plenty of close-ups. I think he is against it mainly because in many cases it signifies a kind of cheaply cobbled together TV production where the camerawork isn't deliberately planned out but more geared to pick up certain moments in a live performance. Consider [this zoom](https://youtu.be/xhaKsgjbt1o?t=108) from a random I Love Lucy sketch. The cameras in such productions zoom around a lot. This is what I assume Godard had in mind (OPs clip is definitely from either late 50's or early 60's, I Love Lucy is from the 50's). 

I feel like even deliberately planned zooms are often fairly cheap but directors like Bava or Fuller play into that cheapness so much that it's interesting again. Their films don't just lack subtlety, they purposefully trample on sublety with their feet. 

The slow zoom which Kubrick uses quite a bit I think is less cheap and can help evoke aural qualities of a scene in for instance the slow reveal or non-reveal of a characters surroundings starting in a close-up shot (there's a lot of that in Lyndon). It has the advantage of creating a reveal without cutting, which can have a stronger effect. I don't really think Godard is considering this possibility necesarilly but then again he's not one who would faun over Kubrick either.
[removed]

> Plus it was used masterfully in Vertigo and the films of Ophuls.

Are you sure that Ophuls used it a lot or very masterfully? I feel like most of that is dollies or craneshots which may sometimes be aided by zooms to retain the framing he wants but it's not always easy to see if there is a zoom involved at all.
I haven't seen his movies for a long time. I must have misremembered.
I think a similar point is when Fritz Lang's character in Le Mepris (shot in 2.35:1) says something along the lines of cinemascope only being useful for filming funerals and snakes.

Really, zoom is a stylistic tool that works in the right circumstances, and I've seen some great examples. Personally I think zooms should be avoided most of the time unless they're slow, subtle movements. Fast zooms call attention to themselves, which can be distracting if they're not an important part of the message.

Godard has always been kind of an ass. Many opinions, many inconsistencies, many extreme tales that amount to a modern edgelord. So him hating zooms, even though he used them, makes sense. I don't think he made much after the 70s truly worth being seen, while others from the french new wave, even though they may have not been as relevant as they were in their prime years, still made good films.

It calls to mind Barry Lyndon where zooms are the antithesis of what you might expect in a period production because they seem so mechanical yet they are used in a way that is opposite to the convention: slow stately zooms that seem to further distance you from the action and individuals by emphasising context, rather than dynamically drawing you in. 

I imagine this very purposeful use of zooms in an unconventional way is not what Godard had in mind and it just goes to show that every tool can be used meaningfully by an artist filmmaker - although he probably disliked Kubrick.

> He's saying, have artistic principles, don't do stuff just because it's trendy or expedient.

This is just so univerally true in many fields.  Like currently our dev team is getting hit with requests to "Add AI" to our various apps and web sites.  A solution in search of a problem.

This essay just highlights how much i hate that "camera is supposed to be invisible" way of thinking a lot of industry people employ. Some of my favorite films are daring with camera movements and shot design. Something like Hard to Be a God (2013) or On the Silver Globe (1979) is better BECAUSE the camera moves so much, and you the viewer notice it. It transports you to a different world where we(the camera) are basically as useful as the other people on screen: not very. Immersion in a story does not require static camera, nor am i saying an evermoving camera is superior, it all just comes down to the skill and planning of those handling the camera.

I hate Godard, which in itself is a blasphemy in the world of cinema. But just as I must have the guts to call his movies trash, he must have the guts to make statements such as this one. True artists tend to have strong opinions and not care what resonance they might cause with them. In this aspect, ironically, I have respect for Godard.

That I Love Lucy clip looks like a push, not a zoom. The end result is somewhat similar but produces different emotional/technical effects, and I'm not sure if Goddard is only referring to one or the other.

I feel like it's hard to say because it's a small zoom and the background is so close anyway. The reason I think it's a zoom is because there's a live audience watching it and having cameras move all around would probably be disturbing.

Imagine *The Conversation* without zooms, or *McCabe and Mrs. Miller,* they would not be the same films. 

Yes it is true that using zooms as a "lazy" substitute for physically moving the camera is bad, of course it is! But as long as Zooms are treated as their own thing with their own unique qualities there is nothing wrong with them whatsoever.

I want to chime in with a slightly different take on his take. 

Everything has its time and place, sure. But I sympathize with his sentiment. Here’s why:

There’s a ton of zooming in found footage, TikTok, and content mills,largely because in film language, zoom is CAPS LOCK. 

Of course, it’s TOOLS not RULES. But when we’re talking about FILM as a LITERARY TRADITION, the overuse of ZOOM is equivalent to the overuse of CAPS LOCK. It’s not like you couldn’t READ or WRITE a book with frequently CAPITALIZED words. But for the MOST PART seeing it a FEW TIMES in a book would feel like an adequate amount. Seeing it EVERY OTHER PAGE would feel like OVERKILL, or like you don’t TRUST the reader to distinguish for THEMSELVES what is important, or perhaps that YOU YOURSELF aren’t aware of a such thing as NUANCE.

But that’s just my two cents. As a filmmaker, I’m not a big fan of zooms. They feel completely different from every other type of shot.

It's a push. You can tell by the way the perspective between objects changes, and because zoom lenses weren't heavily used back then. Zooms were popular in the '70s, in a large part, because it was still fresh. 

Three camera sitcoms, a format pioneered by I Love Lucy, had cameras that were moving all the time but didn't block the view of the audience.

Every director has their own opinions & theories. They're all entitled to them but it's subjective whether or not they have a point. Art requires variety & freedom to develop. Restricting or condemning the use of a certain method only limits what others might do with their creativity & unique perspective. People use different techniques in ways we might not predict. There may still be effective & surprising ways to use zooms that haven't been explored. Film-making goes through seasons & trends & what seems passe now may be reinvigorated in the near future.

For example, the use of black & white in films could have disappeared with the innovation of colour - but filmmakers have been finding new ways to use that old technique in ways that enriches their storytelling (Spielberg with Schindler's List, the Sin City adaptation, Pleasantville etc). A creative filmmaker will be able to take something traditional & turn it upside down. Godard might not be the next person to innovate with zooms, but there may be other filmmakers who surprise & delight us.
Basically, you'd be doing a disservice to yourself as a person who enjoys films to accept one expert's viewpoint above all others. You'd be limiting the boundaries of your own creativity & curiosity.

The zoom is different from most camera movements because the others approximate how we look in real life. A pan or a tilt is like standing still and moving your head. Push in, pull out and tracking shots are how things look when you’re walking. The eye can’t zoom, however; it is a thoroughly technological way of looking at the world. It is understandable that Godard, with his passion for immediacy, wouldn’t use it.
